title: Universality Of Kernels On Riemannian Symmetric Spaces
authors: Salem Said, Natha\"el Da Costa, Franziskus Steinert, Cyrus Mostajeran
abstract: ArXiv:2608.00010v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate universality properties of continuous, positive-definite invariant kernels on Riemannian symmetric spaces, providing a unified harmonic-analytic characterization across compact and non-compact settings. In the compact symmetric case, we prove that a continuous, positive-definite invariant kernel is [MATH]-universal if and only if all of its spherical coefficients are strictly positive, a sharpening of classical Bochner-type results. This characterization is extended to compact homogeneous spaces, where universality is shown to be equivalent to the strict positive-definiteness of coefficient matrices arising from a representation-theoretic expansion. In contrast, for non-compact symmetric spaces, we establish that any continuous, positive-definite invariant kernel that is [MATH] and integrable is automatically [MATH]-universal. Our analysis essentially relies on spectral decompositions using spherical functions and group Fourier transforms, in order to provide alternative, harmonic-analytic formulations of universality conditions. Several examples (including kernels on spheres and compact Lie groups, as well as integrable kernels on hyperbolic spaces and symmetric cones) both illustrate the theory and demonstrate practical criteria for constructing universal kernels.
tldr: This paper studies universality of positive-definite invariant kernels on Riemannian symmetric spaces, a topic in harmonic analysis and machine learning theory.
motivation: The paper aims to characterize when invariant kernels are universal for function approximation on symmetric spaces, which is relevant to kernel methods in machine learning.
method: The authors use harmonic analysis, including spherical functions and group Fourier transforms, to derive conditions for universality in compact and non-compact symmetric spaces.
result: They prove that in compact symmetric spaces, universality is equivalent to strict positivity of spherical coefficients, and in non-compact spaces, integrable positive-definite invariant kernels are automatically universal.
conclusion: The results provide practical criteria for constructing universal kernels on symmetric spaces, but the topic is unrelated to the user's research interests in quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.

title: Unique Axiomatisation Of Fractional Integral Operators On The Real Line
authors: Arran Fernandez Ceren \"ozden
abstract: ArXiv:2608.00021v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Cartwright--McMullen theorem (1978) establishes the uniqueness of the Riemann--Liouville family of fractional integral operators on a compact interval [MATH] under a natural set of axioms: inclusion of the classical integral, a semigroup property, positivity, and continuity. By unpacking the proof into its constituent steps and understanding its structure clearly, we provide improvements and extensions of the original result. Firstly, by using some properties of topological groups, we demonstrate that the positivity axiom can be removed with almost no effect on the result. Secondly, we consider a version of the theorem on the whole real line [MATH], with constant of integration [MATH] instead of [MATH], which was mentioned without proof in the 1978 paper. The theorem can be extended to this setting, but it is not trivial to do so: the theory of Fr\'echet spaces must be used, and we introduced a new shift-commutativity axiom to get the density result that we need to extend the proof to spaces of functions and distributions on [MATH] with left-bounded support.
tldr: This paper extends the Cartwright-McMullen uniqueness theorem for fractional integral operators to the real line, removing the positivity axiom and introducing a shift-commutativity axiom.
motivation: The authors aim to improve and extend the classical uniqueness theorem for fractional integrals, which is a purely mathematical result with no direct connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.
method: They analyze the original proof, use topological group properties to remove positivity, and employ Fréchet space theory and a new shift-commutativity axiom to handle the real line case.

title: Discrepancy Theory: An Algorithmic And Geometric Perspective
authors: Aleksandar Nikolov Nikhil Bansal
abstract: ArXiv:2608.00140v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Combinatorial discrepancy theory is a subject with roots in combinatorics, geometry, and number theory, and with numerous applications to mathematics and computer science. At its core, discrepancy theory is about dividing a collection of objects into two parts that are as balanced as possible. For example, given a collection of subsets of a finite universe, we may wish to color the elements with two colors so that each set is approximately evenly split. Other problems in discrepancy are more geometric in flavor, and ask for example, to assign signs to a collection of vectors, so that the sum of the signed vectors is as small as possible. Classical results, such as the Beck-Fiala theorem and Spencer's "six deviations" result, show that it is often possible to attain remarkably small discrepancy, often far smaller than what naive random colorings achieve. In recent years, discrepancy theory has undergone a transformation, driven by new algorithmic techniques and a rich interplay between probability, optimization, and convex geometry. These developments have led not only to new constructive proofs of foundational theorems, but also to several new results and research directions. This monograph aims to provide an accessible and unified introduction to these modern developments, with a focus on the core algorithmic and convex geometric ideas that have driven them. For several results, we provide new simpler analyses, while highlighting the intuition behind the proofs.
tldr: This paper is a monograph on combinatorial discrepancy theory, focusing on algorithmic and geometric perspectives, with no connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: The paper aims to provide an accessible introduction to modern developments in discrepancy theory, driven by new algorithmic techniques and interplay with probability, optimization, and convex geometry.
method: It presents classical results (Beck-Fiala, Spencer) and new constructive proofs, highlighting algorithmic and convex geometric ideas.
result: The monograph offers unified treatments and new simpler analyses for several results in discrepancy theory.
conclusion: The paper contributes to mathematics and computer science but is unrelated to the user's research interests in quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.

We prove lower bounds on the non-adaptive randomized approximation error with a joint dependence on [MATH] matching previously known upper bounds.

title: The Quaternionic Moment Problem
authors: R. Ben Taher (department Of Mathematics, Faculty Of Sciences, Moulay Ismail University, Meknes, Morocco), K. Schm\"udgen (department Of Mathematics, University Of Leipzig, Leipzig, Germany), E. H. Zerouali
abstract: ArXiv:2608.00188v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper we develop an approach to the full quaternionic moment problem. We define a hierarchy [MATH], [MATH], of two-sided [MATH]-linear spaces of quaternionic polynomials which are invariant under conjugation of quaternions and determine the hermitian parts of these spaces explicitly. Using a generalization of Choquet's theorem on adapted spaces to quaternions we provide necessary and sufficient solvability criteria for the quaternionic moment problem of each space [MATH]. The hermitian part of [MATH] is the real polynomial algebra [MATH]. This enables us to apply real algebraic geometry (Positivstellens\"{a}tze) to the quaternionic moment problem on [MATH].
tldr: This paper develops a mathematical framework for solving the quaternionic moment problem using adapted spaces and Choquet's theorem.
motivation: The quaternionic moment problem is a fundamental question in noncommutative analysis, and the authors aim to provide a complete solution by extending classical techniques to the quaternionic setting.
method: The authors define a hierarchy of two-sided linear spaces of quaternionic polynomials invariant under conjugation, determine their hermitian parts, and use a generalization of Choquet's theorem to derive solvability criteria.

title: On The Asymptotics Of Item Selection In Multidimensional Computerized Adaptive Testing
authors: Xiaoou Li Seungwon Lee
abstract: ArXiv:2608.00201v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study Fisher-information-based item-selection rules for multidimensional computerized adaptive testing (MCAT) with intentional and nuisance abilities. Although such rules are widely used, rigorous asymptotic theory for the coupled dynamics of adaptive selection and latent-trait estimation remains limited. We consider a weighted A-optimality criterion that prioritizes intentional abilities while controlling accuracy in nuisance dimensions. For the multidimensional two-parameter logistic model, we first establish asymptotic optimality under an item-type reuse regime: paired with the maximum likelihood estimator, the weighted A-optimal rule attains the minimum asymptotic weighted mean squared error. We then prove consistency and asymptotic normality of the maximum likelihood estimator and express its asymptotic weighted mean squared error through a limiting Fisher information matrix. We also extend the analysis to the operational setting in which each item is administered at most once. These results justify normal approximations and information-based standard errors in MCAT. A simulation study examines finite-sample behavior at practical test lengths and shows favorable weighted mean squared error, with item-selection patterns consistent with the predicted limiting behavior.
tldr: This paper develops asymptotic theory for item selection in multidimensional computerized adaptive testing, a statistical psychometrics topic unrelated to quantum information.
motivation: The paper addresses a gap in rigorous asymptotic theory for adaptive testing algorithms, which are widely used but lack theoretical guarantees.
method: The authors analyze Fisher-information-based item selection rules under a weighted A-optimality criterion, proving asymptotic optimality and establishing consistency and asymptotic normality of the maximum likelihood estimator.
result: They show that the weighted A-optimal rule achieves minimum asymptotic weighted mean squared error under item-type reuse and extend results to the no-reuse setting, with simulations confirming finite-sample behavior.
conclusion: The work provides theoretical justification for normal approximations and information-based standard errors in MCAT, but it is entirely outside the scope of quantum information science.

title: Regularized-Likelihood Deconvolution With Posterior-Density Reconstruction
authors: Marco Di Marzio, Stefania Fensore, Chiara Passamonti, Serena Pulcini
abstract: ArXiv:2608.00240v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Density deconvolution is an ill-posed inverse problem, as recovering the latent distribution amplifies high-frequency noise in the observed data. We propose a two-stage likelihood-based procedure. The first estimator maximizes the convolution likelihood over a regularized Gaussian-mixture sieve, while the second reuses the fitted density as an empirical prior and averages the resulting conditional latent densities over the observations. The two estimators have different population targets under misspecification: posterior reconstruction locally contracts misspecification bias under identifiable convolution, but introduces an additional first-order variance component under correct finite-dimensional specification. We establish observed- and latent-domain convergence rates under Gaussian error. Under ordinary-smooth error, the direct estimator in [MATH] and the posterior reconstruction in [MATH] attain the classical deconvolution exponent, up to logarithmic factors. Numerical experiments and an application to Framingham blood-pressure data illustrate their complementary finite-sample behavior.
tldr: This paper proposes a two-stage likelihood-based deconvolution method for density estimation, focusing on statistical methodology rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: Density deconvolution is an ill-posed inverse problem, and the authors aim to improve estimation by combining regularized likelihood with posterior reconstruction.
method: The first stage maximizes a regularized Gaussian-mixture likelihood; the second uses the fitted density as an empirical prior to average conditional latent densities.
result: The method achieves classical deconvolution rates under ordinary-smooth error and shows complementary finite-sample behavior in experiments.
conclusion: The proposed approach offers a novel statistical technique for density deconvolution, but it is unrelated to the specified research directions.

title: Approximating The Fourier Transform From Non-equispaced Discrete Samples
authors: Laura Weidensager Daniel Potts
abstract: ArXiv:2608.00260v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the approximation of the Fourier transform of a function from finitely many samples. Departing from the equispaced setting, we sample the function at deterministic non-equispaced nodes obtained by transforming equispaced points on [MATH] through the inverse cumulative distribution function of a probability density. This change of variables compactifies the real line, so that no truncation of the space domain is necessary. Combining an exact aliasing identity for the midpoint rule with stationary-phase estimates for the transformed oscillatory integrals, we derive deterministic error bounds for every frequency and in [MATH]. For functions with polynomial decay in space and frequency, an explicitly optimized density recovers the equispaced convergence rate, while an additional variance parameter substantially reduces the pre-asymptotic error constants. For (sub-)exponentially decaying functions a polynomially decaying density yields (sub-)exponential rates. Numerical experiments confirm the theory and demonstrate the reduced pre-asymptotic error compared with optimally scaled equispaced sampling.
tldr: This paper studies the approximation of Fourier transforms from non-equispaced samples using a change of variables and stationary-phase estimates, with no connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: The paper addresses a classical numerical analysis problem: approximating Fourier transforms from non-uniform samples without truncating the domain.
method: It transforms equispaced points via the inverse CDF of a probability density, derives error bounds using an aliasing identity and stationary-phase estimates, and optimizes the density for convergence rates.

conclusion: The proposed method improves pre-asymptotic error constants compared to equispaced sampling, but the topic is unrelated to the user's research interests.

title: Persistent Mean Tracking In Client--Server Open Networks
authors: Amit Dutta, Fat-Hy Omar Rajab, Marcos M. Vasconcelos, Olugbenga M. Anubi
abstract: ArXiv:2608.00327v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study persistent-agent identification and mean tracking in an open client-server network where agents participate intermittently. The network consists of a core of highly regular persistent agents and a subset of transient/non-persistent agents that appear only sporadically. Since the server observes only binary activity indicators and scalar updates from active agents, naive averaging cannot recover the active persistent mean because transient-agent updates contaminate the aggregate, and heterogeneous participation introduces bias. To address this, we propose a two-phase estimation framework. In Phase I, we develop a two-layer window-based identification procedure: the first layer forms single-window activity decisions, while the second aggregates these decisions across windows to create a high-probability separation between persistent and transient agents. Under heterogeneous Bernoulli participation, we derive explicit finite-window bounds that specify how many windows the server must wait for this separation to occur with high probability. In Phase II, we use the resulting structural estimate to track the active persistent mean via a smoothing filter, and show that the tracking error contracts geometrically to a neighborhood determined by the target drift and the filter gain. We provide numerical simulations to illustrate the effectiveness of our theoretical results.
tldr: This paper studies persistent-agent identification and mean tracking in open client-server networks, which is a topic in distributed estimation and network analysis, not quantum information.
motivation: The authors aim to recover the mean of persistent agents in a network with transient participants, addressing contamination and bias from sporadic agents.
method: They propose a two-phase framework: Phase I uses a two-layer window-based identification to separate persistent from transient agents with finite-window bounds; Phase II applies a smoothing filter to track the persistent mean.
result: They derive finite-window bounds for separation and show geometric contraction of tracking error to a neighborhood determined by drift and filter gain, with numerical simulations.
conclusion: The paper provides a theoretical and numerical solution for mean tracking in open networks, but it is unrelated to the user's research interests in quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.

title: Extinction Thresholds In A Graph-based Model Of Hiv Infection Dynamics
authors: Manuel A. Espinosa-Garc\'ia, Ana Paulina Figueroa, Juli\'an A. Fres\'an-Figueroa, Gerardo L. Maldonado, L. Ariadna S\'anchez-Sol\'is
abstract: ArXiv:2608.00340v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study a graph-based cellular automaton for HIV infection dynamics in lymph-node networks, originally introduced by Mukwembi. Each vertex represents a cell site that may be healthy, infected, or dead, and the evolution is controlled by a replacement parameter [MATH], which determines whether a dead cell is replaced by an infected or a healthy cell according to the number of its infected neighbors. For a graph [MATH], we introduce two extinction parameters. The parameter [MATH] is the smallest value of [MATH] for which extinction occurs for every admissible initial configuration, whereas [MATH] is the smallest threshold such that extinction occurs for every replacement parameter greater than or equal to it. We prove the general bounds [MATH] and characterize the extremal case [MATH]. We also show that the gap [MATH] is unbounded and determine both parameters for some classical families of graphs. Finally, we study the dynamics of the model using the state-transition digraph of the system and the configurations whose trajectories converge to nontrivial periodic orbits. The results show that extinction depends not only on the replacement parameter but also on the structural properties of the underlying graph.

title: Source Reliability Weighted Observer Design For Open Client Server Networks
authors: Amit Dutta, Marcos M. Vasconcelos, Olugbenga M. Anubi
abstract: ArXiv:2608.00342v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: State estimation in open client server networks is challenging because the set of active observation sources changes over time, and active sources need not be valid sensors of the latent state. We study a client-server estimation problem in which a fixed but unknown state-consistent sensing class measures the latent state when active, while nuisance sources may arrive in the active set and generate observations from a different signal class. The server observes active sources, but it does not know which agents observe valid state measurements. We propose a source-reliability-weighted observer. The state estimate is a standard fixed-prior weighted least-squares update, but the information assigned to each active observation is determined by a source-level reliability score learned from repeated innovation consistency. Numerical results show that the observer, when all active sources are considered, has a finite bias, while the proposed observer initially learns source reliability and then tracks the desired latent state after a finite learning period.
tldr: This paper proposes a source-reliability-weighted observer for state estimation in open client-server networks with unreliable observation sources.
motivation: State estimation in open client-server networks is challenging because active sources may not be valid sensors, and the set of active sources changes over time.
method: The proposed observer uses a weighted least-squares update where each observation's weight is determined by a learned source-level reliability score based on innovation consistency.
result: Numerical results show that the proposed observer learns source reliability and tracks the latent state after a finite learning period, unlike a standard observer which has finite bias.
conclusion: The source-reliability-weighted observer effectively handles unreliable sources in open networks, improving state estimation accuracy.

title: Sylvester's Theorem And Reduced Linear Systems: From Three-Factor Products To Small Dynamical Models
authors: James M. Hyman
abstract: ArXiv:2608.00367v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large systems of linear equations often contain far fewer active degrees of freedom than their ambient dimension suggests. A particularly transparent instance occurs when a large matrix factors as A = TSW, where T is m x n, S is n x n, and W is n x m, and m >> n. The action of A then passes through an n-dimensional intermediate space. Sylvester's theorem relates the nonzero eigenvalues of a product XY to those of the reversed product YX. Applied cyclically, it shows that the nonzero spectrum of the large matrix A is completely determined by either of the small matrices B = (WT)S, C = S(WT). This article develops the theorem from first principles and explains the geometry behind the factorization. The result yields exact reduced systems, both for linear algebraic equations and for first-order linear ordinary differential equations. Worked examples carry this through in detail: spectral reduction, reconstruction of full-space eigenvectors, reduced solution of shifted systems, and exact integration of a three-dimensional ODE through a two-dimensional model. A separate section takes up singular values. Those of A, B, and C do not agree in general, though they do when the bases are orthonormal, a case the same theorem settles once it is applied to A*A. The closing sections separate exact factorization from projection-based approximation, and flag what the theorem leaves undetermined: zero-eigenvalue structure, conditioning, and transient behavior. The material is classical. What this article adds is one continuous development, from first principles through to the limits of the theorem, pitched for an upper-level undergraduate course.
tldr: This paper presents a pedagogical development of Sylvester's theorem for reduced linear systems, focusing on exact factorization and spectral reduction, with no connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: The paper aims to provide a self-contained exposition of Sylvester's theorem and its application to reducing large linear systems, targeting an upper-level undergraduate course.
method: The author develops the theorem from first principles, explains the geometry of the factorization A = TSW, and applies it to linear algebraic equations and ODEs, including singular value analysis.
result: The theorem yields exact reduced systems for linear equations and ODEs, with examples showing spectral reduction and reconstruction of eigenvectors, but singular values of A, B, C do not generally agree.
conclusion: The paper is a classical mathematical exposition with no relevance to the user's research interests in quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.

title: Exact Detection Threshold Of The Packing Test
authors: Tuan Pham
abstract: ArXiv:2608.00445v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Using Poisson approximation techniques, we derive the detection threshold of the packing test in when testing spherical uniformity under high-dimensional Fisher--von Mises--Langevin (FvML) and Watson alternatives. Our result rigorously confirms the empirical observation that the packing test is strictly suboptimal for testing uniformity in these two popular models. In the high-dimensional FvML model, its detection threshold is precisely \(\kappa=\Theta\lb p^{3/4}/(\log n)^{1/4}\rb\). In the high-dimensional Watson model, its detection threshold is \(p-2\kappa=\Theta()\), or equivalently \(\kappa=p/2-\Theta()\). The non-null limiting distributions of the packing test under these two models are derived. We show that the limiting scalings of the largest squared inner product undergo a discontinuous phase transition in the Watson model, whereas no analogous phenomenon occurs in the FvML model.
tldr: This paper derives exact detection thresholds for the packing test in high-dimensional spherical uniformity testing under FvML and Watson alternatives, showing its suboptimality.
motivation: The packing test is a known method for testing spherical uniformity, but its theoretical detection threshold was not rigorously established, and empirical evidence suggested it is suboptimal.
method: The author uses Poisson approximation techniques to analyze the distribution of the largest squared inner product under the null and alternative hypotheses, deriving the detection thresholds and non-null limiting distributions.
result: The detection threshold for the FvML model is κ=Θ(p^{3/4}/(log n)^{1/4}), and for the Watson model it is p-2κ=Θ(1) (or κ=p/2-Θ(1)). A discontinuous phase transition in the limiting scaling is found for the Watson model but not for FvML.
conclusion: The packing test is strictly suboptimal for testing uniformity in these high-dimensional models, and the derived thresholds provide a rigorous theoretical foundation for this observation.

title: On The Log Determinant Of Sample Correlation Matrices Under Gaussianity
authors: Hongru Zhao
abstract: ArXiv:2608.00565v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove a central limit theorem for the log determinant of a Gaussian Pearson sample correlation matrix as the dimension diverges. Only two conditions are imposed: the population correlation matrix is positive definite, and the sample degrees of freedom are at least the dimension. Both are necessary for the ordinary log determinant to be finite. To the best of our knowledge, no previous central limit theorem covers this full nonsingular domain. It covers every aspect ratio from dilute growth to the square hard edge. No uniform lower or upper bound is imposed on the eigenvalues of the population correlation matrices: the smallest may approach zero and the largest may diverge. The proof develops a coordinatewise Wiener chaos reduction for the random diagonal normalization and combines it with an exact Wishart transform comparison. Geometrically, the statistic is twice the log volume of a random parallelotope spanned by standardized Gaussian coordinate vectors.
tldr: This paper proves a central limit theorem for the log determinant of Gaussian sample correlation matrices under minimal conditions.
motivation: The log determinant of sample correlation matrices is a fundamental statistic in multivariate statistics, and understanding its asymptotic distribution is important for inference. Previous results required restrictive assumptions on the population eigenvalues or aspect ratio.
method: The proof uses a coordinatewise Wiener chaos reduction for the random diagonal normalization and combines it with an exact Wishart transform comparison.
result: The central limit theorem holds for all aspect ratios from dilute growth to the square hard edge, without uniform bounds on the population eigenvalues, as long as the population correlation matrix is positive definite and the sample degrees of freedom are at least the dimension.
conclusion: This provides a complete characterization of the asymptotic normality of the log determinant in the nonsingular domain, filling a gap in the literature.

title: Empirical Optimal Transport Potentials: Fast Rates And A Functional Central Limit Theorem
authors: Alberto Gonz\'alez-Sanz, Gilles Mordant, Shunan Sheng
abstract: ArXiv:2608.00649v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Optimal transport potentials are fundamental objects in statistics, economics, and machine learning: their gradients generate optimal transport maps, while the potentials themselves act as location-dependent dual prices and sensitivity variables. We study the estimation of the quadratic optimal transport potential when a fixed absolutely continuous reference distribution [MATH] is transported to an unknown distribution [MATH], accessed to via its empirical measure. Our main ingredient is a stability inequality that controls the [MATH] distance, modulo additive constants, between a strongly convex potential [MATH] and a convex potential [MATH] by a weak dual norm of [MATH] together with a second-order Wasserstein remainder of logarithmic type. This separation between the leading empirical-process term and the Wasserstein remainder yields faster convergence for potentials than for the corresponding transport maps. Under smoothness and uniform convexity assumptions, the exact semidiscrete Brenier potential converges in [MATH] at rate [MATH] for [MATH], at rate [MATH] for [MATH], and at rate [MATH] for [MATH]. The polynomial exponents are sharp. In dimensions [MATH], we further establish a nondegenerate function-space central limit theorem and prove consistency of the nonparametric bootstrap. These results yield joint root-[MATH] inference for every fixed finite collection of normalization-invariant weighted contrasts of the potential, including regional shadow premia in reference-based risk problems. Finally, we prove matching upper and lower bounds of order [MATH] for the normalization-invariant sum of the entropic dual potentials.
tldr: This paper studies the statistical estimation of optimal transport potentials, deriving convergence rates and a functional central limit theorem.
motivation: Optimal transport potentials are important in statistics and economics, but their estimation theory is less developed than that of transport maps.
method: The authors use a stability inequality to separate the empirical process term from a Wasserstein remainder, and analyze the convergence of semidiscrete Brenier potentials under smoothness and convexity assumptions.
result: They obtain sharp convergence rates for the potential in various norms, establish a nondegenerate functional central limit theorem in low dimensions, and prove matching bounds for entropic dual potentials.
conclusion: The work provides a rigorous statistical theory for estimating optimal transport potentials, with implications for inference on dual prices and risk measures.

title: On Separable And Frobenius Cowreaths Of Type $(a \otimes H^{\mathrm{op}}, H,\psi)$
authors: Fabio Renda
abstract: ArXiv:2608.00676v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cowreaths of type [MATH] have been investigated in [10,19-21,27] as examples of (h-)separable and Frobenius coalgebras in monoidal categories. They are entwining structures built from a Hopf algebra [MATH] and an [MATH]-comodule algebra [MATH]. In this article we develop a general theory that allows us to recover results from the aforementioned papers in an easier way and also to extend them to cowreaths in higher dimension. Focusing on separability, the crucial observation is that, when [MATH] has bijective antipode, one should work with integrals on the coalgebra [MATH] in place of Casimir morphisms, for they are easier to classify. On the other hand, in dealing with Frobenius properties, we obtain that a cowreath [MATH] is Frobenius if and only if the morphism [MATH] is inner ([MATH] is the distinguished grouplike element in [MATH]). While Frobenius cowreaths are always (h-)separable, examples of (h-)separable cowreaths that are not Frobenius will be presented at the end of this article.
tldr: This paper develops a general theory for separable and Frobenius cowreaths of type (A⊗H^op, H, ψ) in monoidal categories, extending previous results to higher dimensions.
motivation: The author aims to unify and simplify existing results on cowreaths as examples of separable and Frobenius coalgebras, and to extend them to higher-dimensional cases.
method: The paper introduces a general framework using integrals on the coalgebra when the Hopf algebra has bijective antipode, and characterizes Frobenius cowreaths via inner morphisms involving the distinguished grouplike element.
result: It provides easier proofs of known results and new characterizations: a cowreath is Frobenius iff a certain morphism is inner, and examples of separable but not Frobenius cowreaths are given.
conclusion: The work advances the algebraic theory of cowreaths, but it is not connected to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Quantitative Particle Approximation For Controlled Nonlinear Filtering
authors: Erhan Bayraktar, Ibrahim Ekren, Xihao He, Xin Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2608.00686v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We estimate convergence rates of value functions for particle approximations of a controlled nonlinear filtering problem. The state is a McKean--Vlasov diffusion on the flat torus, driven by hidden idiosyncratic noise and observed common noise. The filter---the conditional law of the state given the observations---serves as the state variable of the control problem, and the associated value function solves a second-order Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman equation on the Wasserstein space. We approximate this problem by a centralized \(N\)-particle control problem with independent idiosyncratic noises and a common observation noise. The framework accommodates nonseparable rewards and controlled drifts. Since a single control is applied to the entire population, the Hamiltonian is defined by an optimization performed after integration over the population. Under smoothness of the data, uniform ellipticity, and regularity of this Hamiltonian, we establish uniform value-function error bounds of order \(N^{-1/6}\) for \(d=1\), \(N^{-1/6}(\log N)^{1/3}\) for \(d=2\), and \(N^{-1/(3d)}\) for \(d>2\). The proof combines a translation lift in the common-noise direction, Fourier--Wasserstein inf- and sup-convolutions, viscosity comparison, and particle derivative estimates uniform in \(N\).
tldr: This paper analyzes convergence rates for particle approximations of a controlled nonlinear filtering problem with McKean-Vlasov dynamics, which is a topic in stochastic control and filtering theory, not quantum information.
motivation: The paper aims to provide quantitative error bounds for approximating the value function of a controlled nonlinear filtering problem using particle methods, which is important for numerical implementations.
method: The authors use a centralized N-particle control problem, combine translation lifts, Fourier-Wasserstein inf/sup-convolutions, viscosity comparison, and particle derivative estimates to derive uniform error bounds.
result: They establish value-function error bounds of order N^{-1/6} for d=1, N^{-1/6}(log N)^{1/3} for d=2, and N^{-1/(3d)} for d>2.
conclusion: The paper contributes to stochastic control and filtering theory, but it is unrelated to the user's research interests in quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.

title: Optimal Integral Representations In Projective Tensor Products: Countability And Topology
authors: Mingu Jung
abstract: ArXiv:2608.00709v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study optimal integral representations in projective tensor products, focusing on two questions: whether they can always be replaced by countable optimal decompositions, and whether the resulting notion depends on the Borel topology used on the product of the unit balls. We show that every infinite-dimensional Banach space [MATH] admits an equivalent norm for which, denoting the resulting space by [MATH], there exists an affine homeomorphic embedding \[ \Psi : ([0,1]) \to S_{Z \widehat\otimes_{\pi} Z} \] such that [MATH] and \[ \Psi (\alpha) \in _\pi(Z \widehat\otimes_{\pi} Z) \iff . \] In particular, this implies that there exists a tensor \[ u \in _{\pi}(Z\widehat\otimes_{\pi} Z) \setminus _{\pi}(Z\widehat\otimes_{\pi} Z) \] and the witnessing measure may be chosen to be a nonatomic Radon probability measure. The construction realizes an affine copy of [MATH] as an exposed face of [MATH] and compares the diagonal Lebesgue coupling with countable mixtures of product measures. We also prove that the norm, weak, and--on dual spaces--weak-star versions of integral projective norm attainment define the same class of tensors. Consequently, every infinite-dimensional separable reflexive Banach space [MATH] with the approximation property admits an equivalent norm such that, for the resulting space [MATH], [MATH].
tldr: This paper studies optimal integral representations in projective tensor products of Banach spaces, focusing on countability and topological aspects.
motivation: The research interests focus on quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, and hybrid systems, none of which relate to functional analysis or Banach space theory.
method: The paper constructs affine homeomorphic embeddings and compares different notions of integral projective norm attainment using Borel topologies and Radon measures.
result: It shows that every infinite-dimensional Banach space admits an equivalent norm with a tensor having an optimal integral representation but no countable one, and that different topologies yield the same class of tensors.
conclusion: The paper contributes to Banach space theory but has no connection to the user's research areas, so it is not relevant.

title: Tensor Probabilistic Model Checking Of Finite-Horizon Markov Chains (Extended Version)
authors: Jianlin Li, Nick Guo, Peter Ye, Yizhou Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2608.00374v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We reexamine the problem of verifying Markov chains with respect to step-bounded reachability probabilities. Prevailing approaches rely on encoding the state-transition matrix using either explicit or symbolic representations. While these approaches are effective for sparse transition dynamics, they scale less favorably in the dense regime. Our insight is to cast probabilistic model checking of Markov chains as computations over dense tensors. This methodology enables the use of off-the-shelf compiler toolchains for optimized execution of these tensor computations on hardware accelerators. We prove the soundness of the methodology of mapping probabilistic model checking to tensor computations. We implement our approach in a tool called Tessa . Empirical evaluation shows that Tessa unlocks massive speedups over state-of-theart methods on selected benchmarks from the literature.
tldr: This paper proposes a tensor-based approach for probabilistic model checking of Markov chains, achieving speedups on hardware accelerators.
motivation: Existing explicit and symbolic methods for verifying Markov chains scale poorly for dense transition matrices, motivating a tensor-based approach.
method: The authors cast probabilistic model checking as dense tensor computations and prove the soundness of this mapping, implementing it in a tool called Tessa.
result: Empirical evaluation shows massive speedups over state-of-the-art methods on selected benchmarks.
conclusion: Tensor-based probabilistic model checking is a promising direction for efficient verification of dense Markov chains.

title: Pretrain On Small Synthetic Data, Scale Large For Free: Symmetry-Aware Foundation Model For Logic Rule Induction
authors: Yin Jun Phua
abstract: ArXiv:2608.00383v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Logical rule induction seeks interpretable rules that transfer across propositional schemas. This requires respecting symmetries: atom naming, example order, polarity flips, and label swap. Enforcing exact symmetry by construction lets one trained inducer scale beyond its training schemas. Our central contribution is a canonical export that decodes a discrete rule from literal scores. It needs no retraining and is exactly equivariant whenever those scores respect the symmetries. We instantiate it on the Neural Rule Inducer, a disjunctive-normal-form (DNF) foundation model that natively respects only example order. We restore the remaining symmetries through architecture, inference, and training. On synthetic stress tests, accuracy on the support labels stays stable at much larger schemas, and rule fidelity on fresh inputs remains above the unmodified model. On real data, accuracy improves most on larger schemas. The exported rule is exact on synthetic full-group tests and on schema-valid real-data tests. This is a mathematical property of the export rather than of a specific model, and we validate it empirically only on the NRI. Enforcing symmetry by construction turns this small-data pretrained model into a reusable, interpretable inducer that transfers to larger schemas.
tldr: This paper introduces a symmetry-aware foundation model for logical rule induction that scales to larger schemas without retraining.
motivation: Logical rule induction requires respecting symmetries to transfer across propositional schemas, but existing models often fail to generalize to larger schemas.
method: The authors propose a canonical export that decodes discrete rules from literal scores, ensuring exact equivariance when scores respect symmetries, and instantiate it on the Neural Rule Inducer with additional architectural, inference, and training modifications.
result: Experiments show stable accuracy on larger synthetic schemas and improved accuracy on real data, with exact rule fidelity on full-group tests.
conclusion: Enforcing symmetry by construction enables a small-data pretrained model to become a reusable, interpretable inducer that transfers to larger schemas.

title: Domain Decoupling Attack: Exploiting The Validation Gap Between Protective Dns And Shared Edge Routing
authors: Weizhe Wang, Minhong Dong, Jinhao Li, Yao Zhang, Hao Liu, Qiang Hu, Tao Luo, Guangquan Xu, Bin Wu
abstract: ArXiv:2608.00643v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Network attackers often conceal malicious communication within legitimate Internet traffic. Existing CDN-based evasion techniques rely on SNI--Host inconsistency, insufficient domain ownership verification, or provider-specific routing rewrites, which limit their applicability in modern CDN environments. We identify a validation gap in DNS-based authorization, where permission derived from an allowed domain applies to a shared IP and can be reused to reach another tenant in both CDN and non-CDN shared-hosting environments. This paper presents the Domain Decoupling Attack (DDA), which resolves an allowed domain to obtain permission for a shared edge IP and subsequently connects to the same address while presenting the hidden domain consistently in both TLS SNI and HTTP Host. Measurements of 1,069,048 domains across six continents produce 18,025,068 successful probes and identify exposure rates of 95.8% overall, 99.26% for CDN domains, 92.75% for non-CDN domains, and 97.7% for non-CDN cross-tenant IPs, while laboratory experiments reveal a structural limitation of DNS-bound access control on shared addresses. These results clarify the security risks of DNS-derived IP authorization and support the evaluation and improvement of access-control mechanisms in CDN and non-CDN shared-hosting environments.
tldr: This paper presents a network security attack exploiting DNS-based authorization gaps in CDN and shared hosting environments.
motivation: To highlight security risks in DNS-derived IP authorization for shared edge routing, which can be abused to access other tenants' resources.
method: The authors identify a validation gap where an allowed domain grants access to a shared IP, then use consistent SNI/Host to reach another tenant, with large-scale measurements and lab experiments.
result: They report high exposure rates (95.8% overall) across CDN and non-CDN domains, demonstrating the widespread vulnerability.
conclusion: The findings clarify the risks of DNS-bound access control and support improving access-control mechanisms in shared hosting environments.

title: Improving The Security Of Containerized Workloads Using Transparency And Traceability Services
authors: Nikos Fotiou, Lefteris Georgiadis, Ignacio Lacalle, George C. Polyzos, Vasilios A. Siris
abstract: ArXiv:2608.00660v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Containerized workloads are commonly built via CI/CD pipelines, stored in registries, and executed across heterogeneous infrastructures, including cloud and edge environments. A single compromised build step or credential can turn routine automation into large-scale distribution of malicious artifacts, motivating integrity, transparency, and enforceable deployment-time checks. In this paper, we present an architecture for verifiable container image distribution that addresses key-management challenges and enables policy-enforced admission-time verification. A transparency service generates one-time signing keys bound to authenticated identities, records signing events in an append-only transparency registry, and returns cryptographically verifiable proofs of inclusion. These proofs and identity attributes are attached to image metadata and evaluated by policy-as-code at admission time, so only compliant artifacts are deployed. We implement a proof-of-concept integrated with GitHub Actions and GitLab Runners and evaluate how the resulting pipeline mitigates common supply-chain attacks under a realistic threat model.
tldr: This paper presents an architecture for verifiable container image distribution using transparency services and policy-as-code, focusing on supply-chain security.
motivation: Containerized workloads are vulnerable to supply-chain attacks, and existing solutions lack robust integrity and traceability mechanisms.
method: The authors design a transparency service that generates one-time signing keys, records signing events in an append-only registry, and attaches proofs of inclusion to image metadata, which are evaluated by policy-as-code at admission time.
result: They implement a proof-of-concept integrated with GitHub Actions and GitLab Runners, demonstrating mitigation of common supply-chain attacks under a realistic threat model.
conclusion: The proposed architecture enhances container image security but is not related to quantum information, thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Supporting Cybersecurity Risk Management For Medical Devices Via The Secuman Ontology And Shapes
authors: Martin Diller, Anne Esslinger, Piotr Gorczyca, Evi Hartig, Lia Kacholdt, Hannes Strass
abstract: ArXiv:2608.00698v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose the SECUMAN ontology and shapes for representing and analysing cybersecurity risk-management documentation for medical devices. Cybersecurity risks are increasingly relevant for connected medical devices and may have direct consequences for patient safety. Current risk-management files are often maintained as semi-structured natural language text, which makes consistency checking, certification review, and reuse difficult. SECUMAN provides a formal OWL-based vocabulary for modelling security-risk context, assessment, control measures, and residual-risk evaluation, and uses SHACL constraints to check structural completeness and conformity with the intended documentation model. The ontology is aligned with VDE Spec 90025 and the related RISKMAN ontology and shapes, while extending their safety-oriented approach to concepts relevant to cybersecurity risk documentation such as threat scenarios, protection goals, attacker profiles, exposure levels, assets, and secure design arguments. SECUMAN is intended to support automated first-pass validation, traceability, and integration of cybersecurity and safety risk-management documentation.
tldr: This paper introduces SECUMAN, an OWL ontology and SHACL shapes for representing and validating cybersecurity risk-management documentation for medical devices.
motivation: Cybersecurity risks in connected medical devices are increasing, but risk-management files are often unstructured text, hindering consistency checking and certification review.
method: The authors develop a formal OWL-based vocabulary aligned with VDE Spec 90025 and RISKMAN, extending it with cybersecurity concepts, and use SHACL constraints to enforce structural completeness.
result: SECUMAN supports automated first-pass validation, traceability, and integration of cybersecurity and safety risk-management documentation.
conclusion: The ontology aims to improve the management and review of cybersecurity risks for medical devices, but it is not related to quantum information or quantum technologies.

title: Hardware-rooted Attestation For AI-agent Evidence: Composing Ietf Rats With Action Evidence Packages
authors: Anton Sokolov
abstract: ArXiv:2608.00801v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: An action evidence package (AEP) is a signed, append-only record of what an AI agent did, who or what authorised the action, and what the outcome was. It is a software-layer artefact: it tells a verifier the story of an action as the agent's own runtime reports it. This note argues that software attestation of this kind is necessary but not sufficient. When a verifier's question shifts from "what does the agent claim it did?" to "did the specific model version the operator claims to have deployed actually produce this output, on unmodified hardware?", the AEP alone cannot answer. The missing element is a hardware root of trust: an attestation that the measured boot and runtime state of the platform match an endorsed reference. The IETF Remote Attestation Procedures (RATS) architecture (RFC 9334) and Veraison, an open-source RATS Verifier implementation (Confidential Computing Consortium / Linux Foundation), supply exactly this. We propose a composite attestation: hardware Evidence appraised under RATS, bound to a software AEP. We map a small verifier vocabulary (Authorised / Unauthorised / Indeterminate / Attested / Contested / Expired) onto RATS appraisal outcomes, and demonstrate feasibility with a small executed experiment: on a software Trusted Platform Module (TPM; the swtpm emulator), an output-binding protocol folds the hash of an AEP outcome and a fresh appraiser nonce into an attestation-key-signed quote, with a model-artefact measurement carried in a platform register. A minimal RATS-Verifier stand-in resolves the three platform outcomes as designed -- Attested for a good, fresh quote; Contested when the model measurement is swapped; Expired when a stale quote is replayed -- and rejects a forged AEP outcome bound to a valid quote. The result is a feasibility demonstration on emulated hardware, not a hardware-rooted guarantee.
tldr: This paper proposes a composite attestation architecture combining IETF RATS hardware attestation with software action evidence packages for AI agents, demonstrated on emulated TPM.
motivation: Software-only attestation of AI agent actions is insufficient to prove that a specific model on unmodified hardware produced an output; a hardware root of trust is needed.
method: The authors map verifier outcomes to RATS appraisal results and implement a proof-of-concept using swtpm, binding an AEP hash and nonce into a TPM quote with model measurement in a PCR.
result: The prototype correctly distinguishes Attested, Contested, and Expired states, and rejects forged AEPs, but only on emulated hardware.
conclusion: The approach is feasible but not yet a hardware-rooted guarantee; further work is needed for real TPMs and integration.

title: Freemium Is All You Need
authors: Aviv Yaish Maxim Bichuch
abstract: ArXiv:2608.00823v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Free access to a generative AI (GenAI) service requires costly compute, yet can also produce data that improve future service quality. We study a service provider whose users differ in request value and privacy preference, under the constraint that paid requests are kept private, while free requests can be used to improve model quality which otherwise reverts toward a baseline. In particular, we characterize service demand and prove that quality converges to a unique steady state for every stationary service strategy. Next, we analyze optimal pricing and quality policies and show that these can be expressed using two endogenous user value thresholds. For uniform values, we provide a closed-form optimal service strategy and characterize the sufficient conditions for offering free services as dependent on inference cost.
tldr: This paper analyzes optimal pricing and quality policies for a generative AI service with free and paid tiers, focusing on user privacy and model improvement.
motivation: The authors aim to understand how a service provider can balance the costs of free access against the benefits of data collection for model improvement, while respecting user privacy preferences.
method: They model user demand with heterogeneous values and privacy preferences, prove convergence of service quality to a steady state, and derive optimal pricing and quality policies using threshold-based analysis.
result: They characterize optimal policies via two endogenous user value thresholds and provide a closed-form solution for uniform value distributions, showing conditions under which free service is offered.
conclusion: The work provides insights into the economics of generative AI services, but it is not related to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Xr-prism: Data-Driven Privacy And Risk Impact Scoring Metric For Extended Reality In Healthcare
authors: M. Rasel Mahmud Nafisa Anjum
abstract: ArXiv:2608.00826v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Extended Reality (XR) technologies are transforming healthcare through immersive training, remote consultation, and patient rehabilitation. However, their extensive sensing capabilities and complex data pipelines introduce distinct security, privacy, and safety risks. Existing research lacks a unified quantitative framework for assessing and prioritizing these risks. We review 65 peer-reviewed studies on XR security and privacy published from 2017 to 2024, synthesizing a four-layer threat taxonomy consisting of Device, Network, User, and Cloud layers, along with a corresponding catalog of defenses. Building on this analysis, we introduce XR-PRISM, a six-factor weighted Privacy and Risk Impact Scoring Metric that integrates threat likelihood, system vulnerability, attack surface, safety impact, privacy impact, and control effectiveness into a single actionable risk score. Our analysis shows that more than 70% of the identified countermeasures lack standardized risk evaluation, while fewer than 15% of the documented attacks require a high level of expertise to execute. XR-PRISM provides researchers and practitioners with a transparent, data-driven method for comparing, prioritizing, and mitigating security and privacy risks in healthcare XR deployments.
tldr: This paper introduces XR-PRISM, a data-driven risk scoring metric for security and privacy risks in extended reality (XR) healthcare applications.
motivation: XR technologies in healthcare introduce unique security, privacy, and safety risks, but existing research lacks a unified quantitative framework to assess and prioritize these risks.
method: The authors review 65 peer-reviewed studies on XR security and privacy (2017-2024), synthesize a four-layer threat taxonomy (Device, Network, User, Cloud), and propose a six-factor weighted scoring metric (XR-PRISM) integrating threat likelihood, system vulnerability, attack surface, safety impact, privacy impact, and control effectiveness.
result: The analysis reveals that over 70% of identified countermeasures lack standardized risk evaluation, and fewer than 15% of documented attacks require high expertise. XR-PRISM provides a transparent, data-driven method for comparing and mitigating risks.
conclusion: XR-PRISM offers a practical tool for researchers and practitioners to prioritize security and privacy risks in healthcare XR deployments, addressing a gap in quantitative risk assessment.

title: Discovery Is Not The Opposite Of Application
authors: Hiranya V. Peiris
abstract: ArXiv:2608.00172v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Restructuring research funding as a choice between discovery and application gets the economics wrong, the evidence wrong and the people wrong.
tldr: This paper argues against framing research funding as a dichotomy between discovery and application, citing economic, evidence, and human factors.
motivation: The author challenges the common policy perspective that separates basic and applied research, aiming to correct misconceptions in funding strategies.
method: The paper presents a policy argument based on economic reasoning, empirical evidence, and considerations of the research workforce.
result: It concludes that the discovery-application dichotomy is flawed and that such framing misguides funding decisions.
conclusion: Research funding should integrate discovery and application rather than treat them as opposites.

title: Explicit Description Of Certain 3-point K-theoretic Gromov-Witten Invariants For Flag Manifolds
authors: Daisuke Sagaki Satoshi Naito
abstract: ArXiv:2608.00359v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give an explicit description, in terms of the quantum Bruhat graph, of the (torus-equivariant) 3-point, genus 0, [MATH]-theoretic Gromov-Witten invariants [MATH] for the (full) flag manifold [MATH], where [MATH] denotes the class in the (torus-equivariant) [MATH]-theory ring [MATH] of [MATH] of the line bundle [MATH] over [MATH] associated to a weight [MATH] lying in the Weyl group orbit of a minuscule fundamental weight [MATH], and [MATH], [MATH] are the Schubert and opposite Schubert classes in [MATH] for [MATH]. This result can be thought of as a partial generalization of the quantum [MATH]-theoretic divisor axiom, which we obtained in our previous work; our proof utilizes a generalization of the Chevalley formula in the (torus-equivariant) quantum [MATH]-theory ring [MATH] of [MATH], which computes the quantum product with the line bundle class [MATH] associated to the weight [MATH] above.
tldr: This paper provides explicit formulas for certain 3-point K-theoretic Gromov-Witten invariants on flag manifolds using the quantum Bruhat graph.
motivation: The authors aim to generalize the quantum K-theoretic divisor axiom to a broader class of line bundles, contributing to the understanding of quantum K-theory of flag manifolds.
method: They use a generalization of the Chevalley formula in the torus-equivariant quantum K-theory ring and describe invariants in terms of the quantum Bruhat graph.
result: They obtain explicit descriptions of the invariants for weights in the Weyl group orbit of a minuscule fundamental weight.
conclusion: This work extends previous results and provides a partial generalization of the divisor axiom, with potential applications in algebraic geometry and combinatorics.

title: Exploring Usability And Legal Practice: Insights From German Judicial Users Of Digital Forensics
authors: Tobias Hoppmann, Leona Lassak, M. Angela Sasse, Zinaida Benenson
abstract: ArXiv:2608.00541v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Digital forensics has become an integral part of modern criminal proceedings, yet its effective integration remains challenging because of increasing data volumes, evolving technologies, and complex interactions between technical and legal stakeholders. Although prior work has focused primarily on digital forensic tools and methods, its broader procedural and organizational context has received limited attention. Building on emerging perspectives inspired by usability research and human-centered security, we conceptualize digital forensics as part of a socio-technical system within criminal proceedings. We consequently investigate this perspective through a survey of 101 practitioners from the judiciary of the German federal state of North Rhine-Westphalia, including public prosecutors, judges, and digital forensic experts. The results indicate a strong demand for improved integration of digital forensics into workflows, enhanced cross-domain communication, and a closer alignment of stakeholder expectations. They also uncover great potential for the improvement of digital forensics usability, e.g., through stronger interdisciplinary cooperation, easier and faster access to evidential data and results, or improvement of stakeholder training and education.
tldr: This paper surveys German judicial users of digital forensics to explore usability and legal practice, but it is unrelated to quantum information science.
motivation: The paper addresses the integration of digital forensics in criminal proceedings, focusing on socio-technical aspects and usability, which is outside the scope of quantum information research.
method: The authors conducted a survey of 101 practitioners from the judiciary in North Rhine-Westphalia, including prosecutors, judges, and digital forensic experts.
result: The survey revealed a demand for improved workflow integration, cross-domain communication, and usability enhancements in digital forensics.
conclusion: The paper concludes that digital forensics would benefit from interdisciplinary cooperation and better stakeholder training, but this has no relevance to quantum information.

title: From Chasing Ghosts To Missed Attacks: Perspectives And Perceptions Of Soc Practitioners On Llm Integration, Risks, And Readiness
authors: Jonas Thurner, Nadine Jost, Stefan Albert Horstmann, Fabian Ising, Lea Groeber, Alena Naiakshina, Sebastian Schinzel
abstract: ArXiv:2608.00672v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Security Operations Centers (SOCs) process large volumes of security events, requiring analysts to accurately detect and assess ongoing cyberattacks under time pressure. Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) suggest potential benefits for security operations, yet their practical suitability for real-world SOC workflows remains poorly understood. To address this gap, we conducted 25 semi-structured interviews with SOC practitioners who had prior experience with LLMs, complemented by interactive scenarios to anticipate challenges and identify opportunities for the responsible integration of LLM-based tools into SOC workflows. We identified 15 LLM use cases grouped into six functional categories. While LLMs are valued for automating repetitive, low-level tasks such as report automation, practitioners rate high-impact tasks such as incident analysis as not yet feasible, reporting limitations in technical depth, context awareness, and organization-specific knowledge. They locate these limitations less in the models than in the readiness of their SOCs and human factors driving over-reliance. Despite concerns, practitioners express a strong willingness to adopt LLMs, describing competitive pressure that leaves few alternatives. This work contributes an empirical, practitioner-driven analysis of LLM use across SOC roles and organizations and derives concrete design and integration requirements for human-centered, operationally safe LLM-assisted security operations.
tldr: This paper presents an empirical study on the integration of LLMs into Security Operations Centers, focusing on practitioner perspectives and risks.
motivation: The study aims to understand the practical suitability of LLMs for SOC workflows, given the high volume of security events and the potential benefits of LLMs.
method: The authors conducted 25 semi-structured interviews with SOC practitioners who had LLM experience, complemented by interactive scenarios to identify use cases and challenges.
result: They identified 15 LLM use cases in six categories, finding that LLMs are valued for low-level automation but not yet trusted for high-impact tasks like incident analysis due to limitations in technical depth and context awareness.
conclusion: Practitioners are willing to adopt LLMs despite concerns, driven by competitive pressure, and the paper derives design requirements for human-centered LLM integration in SOCs.

title: Mitigating Ray Effects In Rarefied Flow Simulations Using An Ensemble-of-subproblems Strategy With Stochastic Discrete Velocities
authors: Shuyang Zhang (state Key Laboratory Of Coal Combustion, School Of Energy And Power Engineering, Huazhong University Of Science And Technology, Wuhan, China), Weidong Li (national Key Laboratory Of Aerospace Physics In Fluids, Mianyang, China), Ming Fang (national Key Laboratory Of Aerospace Physics In Fluids, Mianyang, China), Zhaoli Guo
abstract: ArXiv:2608.00514v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this work, a ensemble-of-subproblems strategy with stochastic discrete velocities is extended to deterministic methods for mitigating ray effects in rarefied flow simulations. The strategy involves performing multiple independent subproblems, each using a small set of randomly sampled velocity points, and then averaging their solutions to obtain the final result. The core idea is to ensure that the distribution function at any velocity can contribute to the final result, approximating highly refined velocity-space resolution without increasing the memory requirement in any single subproblem. We incorporate this strategy within the DUGKS framework, and the resulting method is denoted as SDV-DUGKS. To evaluate the performance of the proposed method, we compare SDV-DUGKS with the original DUGKS on several test cases: (a) the Sod shock tube problem, (b) the one-dimensional Riemann problem, (c) the two-dimensional lid-driven cavity flow, and (d) the two-dimensional Riemann problem. The results show that, in the collisionless limit [MATH]: (1) for one-dimensional compressible flows, SDV-DUGKS reduces memory usage by approximately 2/3 compared with that of the original DUGKS while achieving good agreement; (2) for two-dimensional compressible flows, SDV-DUGKS requires one to two orders of magnitude less memory than the original DUGKS while achieving good agreement. Based on these results, it can be concluded that the proposed method serves as a reliable and effective tool for mitigating ray effects in rarefied flow simulations.
tldr: This paper presents a numerical method for mitigating ray effects in rarefied gas flow simulations using an ensemble-of-subproblems strategy with stochastic discrete velocities.
motivation: Ray effects in rarefied flow simulations cause numerical artifacts due to insufficient velocity-space resolution. The authors aim to reduce memory requirements while maintaining accuracy.
method: The method, SDV-DUGKS, extends the ensemble-of-subproblems strategy to the deterministic DUGKS framework. It runs multiple independent subproblems with randomly sampled velocity points and averages their solutions.
result: SDV-DUGKS reduces memory usage by about 2/3 for 1D flows and by one to two orders of magnitude for 2D flows compared to original DUGKS, while achieving good agreement in test cases.
conclusion: The proposed method is a reliable and effective tool for mitigating ray effects in rarefied flow simulations, offering significant memory savings.

title: A Memory-efficient Deterministic Method For Multiscale Gas Flows Using An Ensemble-of-subproblems Strategy With Stochastic Discrete Velocities
authors: Shuyang Zhang (state Key Laboratory Of Coal Combustion, School Of Energy And Power Engineering, Huazhong University Of Science And Technology, Wuhan, China), Weidong Li (national Key Laboratory Of Aerospace Physics In Fluids, Mianyang, China), Ming Fang (national Key Laboratory Of Aerospace Physics In Fluids, Mianyang, China), Zhaoli Guo
abstract: ArXiv:2608.00521v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deterministic multiscale gas flow simulations have long suffered from the curse of dimensionality: the number of discrete velocities increases dramatically with the velocity space dimension and the Mach number, exhausting available memory and computational resources. To address this issue, this paper proposes a memory-efficient deterministic method based on an ensemble-of-subproblems strategy using stochastic discrete velocities. This strategy transforms the originally computationally expensive problem into a series of independently and efficiently solvable subproblems. To be concrete, the proposed method replaces the conventional large deterministic velocity set with multiple small random velocity sets. Each random set defines a subproblem, which is solved by a deterministic multiscale numerical scheme that computes macroscopic moments via Monte Carlo integration. The final flow field is obtained by arithmetic averaging over all sub-problems. In this work, we employ the discrete unified gas kinetic scheme (DUGKS) for spatial discretization and term the resulting method SDV-DUGKS. To validate the proposed method, several numerical test cases are conducted, including (a) the one-dimensional shock structure, (b) the two-dimensional cavity flow, and (c) supersonic flow around a square cylinder. The results of the one-dimensional shock structure confirm the feasibility of the proposed method. The two-dimensional cases demonstrate that, compared to its deterministic counterpart, the proposed method saves more than 80% of memory usage while maintaining comparable accuracy. These results indicate that the proposed method markedly reduces memory demand for multiscale flow simulations and exhibits strong potential to alleviate the curse of dimensionality that currently hinders deterministic multiscale numerical schemes from being applied to engineering problems.
tldr: This paper proposes a memory-efficient deterministic method for multiscale gas flows using stochastic discrete velocities, which is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: The paper addresses the curse of dimensionality in deterministic multiscale gas flow simulations, which is a computational fluid dynamics problem, not a quantum information or thermodynamics topic.
method: The method replaces a large deterministic velocity set with multiple small random velocity sets, solving each subproblem with a deterministic multiscale scheme and averaging results.
result: The method saves over 80% memory in 2D cases while maintaining accuracy, demonstrating feasibility for multiscale flow simulations.
conclusion: The proposed method alleviates memory constraints in multiscale gas flow simulations, but it has no connection to the user's research interests.

title: Gendered Structural Roles In Indian Epics
authors: John D. P. Evans
abstract: ArXiv:2608.00534v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Mahabharata and the Ramayana constitute the two major Sanskrit epics of ancient India. Previous network analysis revealed substantial structural similarities between their character networks, alongside differences consistent with their contrasting forms of narrative organisation. Building upon these findings, we investigate the representation and structural positions of male and female characters within the two texts. In particular, we examine whether the genders differ systematically in their connectivity, prominence, community participation, and contribution to network cohesion, while accounting for the considerable imbalance between the numbers of male and female characters. We employ methods designed to identify characters who connect otherwise distinct regions of the networks and to assess the structural consequences of character removal. Through these analyses, we ask whether gendered patterns are consistent across the two epics or instead reflect the different narrative structures previously identified. In so doing, we find that male characters are considerably more prevalent among highly central and structurally consequential nodes in both epics, and targeted removal of central male characters produces substantially greater network disruption. However, once baseline structural position is taken into account, we find little residual difference in deletion effects between male and female characters. Furthermore, under selected Girvan-Newman partitions, we find that female characters in the Mahabharata exhibit greater cross-community participation than female characters in the Ramayana.
tldr: This paper analyzes gender differences in the structural roles of characters in Indian epics using network analysis.
motivation: The authors aim to understand how gender is represented in ancient Indian narratives through quantitative network analysis.
method: They apply network analysis techniques to character networks from the Mahabharata and Ramayana, examining connectivity, prominence, community participation, and deletion effects.
result: Male characters are more central and structurally consequential, but after controlling for baseline position, gender differences in deletion effects are minimal; female characters in the Mahabharata show more cross-community participation.
conclusion: The study reveals gendered structural patterns in the epics, with implications for understanding narrative and social structures.

title: Beyond Lanes: Traffic Flow Dynamics In Disordered Conditions Based On High-Resolution Trajectory Data
authors: Shrey Agrawal, Gowri Asaithambi, Venkatesan Kanagaraj, Martin Treiber, Ostap Okhrin, Harish Babu Kumara
abstract: ArXiv:2608.00602v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Disordered traffic flow is characterized by weak or non-existent lane discipline in the presence of strong vehicle heterogeneity and continuous lateral interactions, challenging traditional lane-based modeling assumptions. This study presents an empirical study of macroscopic and microscopic aspects of disordered traffic using high-resolution UAV trajectory data collected on an urban arterial. A two-dimensional extension of Edie's framework is applied to quantify aggregate traffic variables and produce a two-dimensional fundamental diagram, revealing that traffic states cannot be adequately represented using one-dimensional formulations and highlighting the persistent role of lateral redistribution. The propagation of congestion is estimated directly from the spatiotemporal speed fields, demonstrating the emergence of coherent stop-and-go waves and showing a similar dynamics as conventional lane-based flow, in spite of the heterogeneous vehicle interactions. At the microscopic level, steady-state follower-leader identification is used to examine desired time gaps and minimum lateral spacing, vehicle dimension distributions, and kinematic characteristics, revealing pronounced inter-class heterogeneity that explains disordered traffic behavior. The study provides an empirical framework linking vehicle-level interactions and aggregate traffic dynamics and establishes a data-driven basis for the calibration and validation of traffic models for disordered mixed traffic systems.
tldr: This paper studies disordered traffic flow using UAV trajectory data, focusing on macroscopic and microscopic traffic dynamics without any quantum information or thermodynamics content.
motivation: The authors aim to understand disordered traffic flow, which is characterized by weak lane discipline and heterogeneous vehicles, challenging traditional lane-based models.
method: They apply a two-dimensional extension of Edie's framework to quantify traffic variables, construct a fundamental diagram, and analyze spatiotemporal speed fields for congestion propagation. Microscopic follower-leader identification is used to examine time gaps, lateral spacing, and vehicle dimensions.
result: The study reveals that one-dimensional traffic representations are inadequate, and that coherent stop-and-go waves emerge despite heterogeneous interactions. Pronounced inter-class heterogeneity explains disordered behavior.
conclusion: The paper provides an empirical framework linking vehicle-level interactions to aggregate traffic dynamics, offering a data-driven basis for calibrating traffic models for disordered mixed traffic.

title: Consistent And Bound-preserving Finite-volume Weno Scheme For Compressible two-/$N$-phase Flows With Phase-Field Mechanism
authors: Ziyang Huang
abstract: ArXiv:2608.00746v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In the present study, we propose a consistent and bound-preserving finite-volume WENO scheme that satisfies the requirements of consistency, conservation, equilibrium, and bound preservation for compressible multiphase flows with the Phase-Field mechanism. The proposed WENO scheme is developed based on a new calculation of WENO weights determined by relative smoothness between stencils and on a coupled reconstruction of the masses and volume fractions. Consistency of reduction and volume fraction summation to unity are considered during the development so that fictitious phases, local voids, or overfilling are not produced numerically when there are [MATH] ([MATH]) different immiscible phases. The proposed WENO scheme is applied to the consistent and conservative Phase-Field method with adaptive mesh refinement enabled. Various benchmark compressible two- and [MATH]-phase flows are performed to verify the properties of the proposed WENO scheme as well as its variant with the consistent limiter. We finally demonstrate the capability of the proposed WENO scheme in shock-induced cavity collapse and shock-vessel-bubble interaction problems, with discussion of the necessity of bound preservation for high-order schemes and comparison of different compressible multiphase flow models.
tldr: This paper proposes a consistent and bound-preserving finite-volume WENO scheme for compressible multiphase flows with phase-field mechanism.
motivation: The paper aims to develop a numerical scheme that satisfies consistency, conservation, equilibrium, and bound preservation for compressible multiphase flows, addressing issues like fictitious phases and local voids.
method: The method introduces a new calculation of WENO weights based on relative smoothness and a coupled reconstruction of masses and volume fractions, integrated with a consistent and conservative phase-field method and adaptive mesh refinement.
result: The scheme is verified on various benchmark compressible two- and N-phase flows, and demonstrated on shock-induced cavity collapse and shock-vessel-bubble interaction problems.
conclusion: The proposed WENO scheme effectively maintains bound preservation and consistency for compressible multiphase flows, highlighting the necessity of bound preservation for high-order schemes.

title: Quaternionic Kittaneh Numerical Radius Inequalities
authors: K. Mahesh Krishna

title: On Non-symmetric $t$-convexity
authors: Paolo Leonetti
abstract: ArXiv:2608.00067v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Zsolt P\'ales asked whether there exists a function [MATH] such that $[MATH]$ which is not midconvex. We show that the answer is negative.
